items.title: Cradle to Cradle
items.claim: Cradle to Cradle (2002) by William McDonough and Michael Braungart argued for what shift in design thinking?

options.text: Design products so materials cycle back as technical or biological nutrients

items.reveal_title: Materials as nutrients in cycles, not waste streams
items.reveal:
The book distinguishes 'technical' cycles (industrial materials recovered indefinitely) from 'biological' cycles (materials safely returning to ecosystems).

The approach informs current discussions of the circular economy and EU eco-design regulations.
items.why: Design intent at the material-choice stage shapes what is possible at end of life.

items.title: Fitts's law
items.claim: Paul Fitts's 1954 model predicts the time to point at a target. What variables does it use?

options.text: Colour and brightness of the target
Distance to target and target width
Number of fingers and finger length

items.reveal_title: Movement time depends on distance over width
items.reveal:
Fitts's law: MT = a + b * log2(2D/W). The model still informs button sizing in user interfaces and the design of touchscreen targets.

Apple Human Interface Guidelines minimum 44pt touch targets descend from this lineage.
items.why: Quantitative models from the 1950s still shape decisions in modern UI design.

items.title: Riveted jeans patent
items.claim: Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis patented riveted denim trousers. In which year?
items.reveal:
Davis, a Nevada tailor, had the rivet idea; Strauss provided the cloth and patent capital. The trouser was a workwear product for miners and labourers for most of its first century.

Global denim production now exceeds 7 billion pairs per year.
items.why: A small mechanical detail can define a category for over 150 years.
